item.title: FASTPANEL VPS Hosting
item.description:
FASTPANEL VPS Hosting combines a self-managed VPS with a web-hosting control panel for websites, domains, databases, PHP, SSL, mail, backups and scheduled jobs. The panel simplifies routine hosting administration, but the VPS still has to be sized for FASTPANEL plus the websites and services running behind it.

VDSina currently lists FASTPANEL on Ubuntu 22 as a web-hosting-control-panel deployment option on its Standard VPS. That is a provider deployment choice, not a claim that the server becomes fully managed.

item.title: How to Choose VPS Location
item.description:
The best VPS location is not automatically the country closest to you. Choose the region around the users and systems that actually exchange latency-sensitive traffic with the server, then verify the real network path before buying.

For most websites, start near the largest or most valuable audience. Then check routing, dynamic traffic, database/API dependencies, CDN behavior and any real data-location requirement.

For the broader VPS decision, see VPS for website.

item.title: How to host a website on VPS
item.description:
How to host a website on VPS depends on the application you are deploying. A static site needs a web server and DNS. WordPress or another PHP CMS also needs PHP and a database. A Node.js or Python application usually runs behind a reverse proxy. You can build those pieces manually on a clean VPS or use a control panel to manage them through a browser.

This guide owns the fresh-VPS-to-live-website workflow. If you are moving an existing production site with live data, use Website migration to VPS for the cutover and rollback process.

item.title: Managed vs Unmanaged VPS
item.description:
Managed vs Unmanaged VPS is mainly a decision about who operates the server after it is provisioned. The virtual machine can have the same CPU, RAM and disk either way. What changes is responsibility for the operating system, security, web stack, backups, monitoring, troubleshooting and recovery.

item.title: VPS Backup Strategy
item.description:
VPS Backup Strategy is not “turn on snapshots once a day.” A usable recovery plan defines how much data you can lose (RPO), how long recovery may take (RTO), which data must survive, where independent copies live, how long versions are retained, and whether anybody has actually restored them.

A strong VPS plan usually combines fast provider-side recovery with an independent off-server copy and application-aware database backups. The exact mix depends on how quickly the data changes and how costly downtime is.

item.title: VPS for Multiple Websites
item.description:
VPS for Multiple Websites works well when several sites can safely share one resource pool, one administration model and one failure domain. The important limit is not the number of domains. It is the combined peak of CPU, RAM, PHP/application workers, database work, storage, background jobs and backups across every site on the server.

For the broader buying decision, see VPS for website.

item.title: VPS for WooCommerce
item.description:
VPS for WooCommerce should be sized for the parts of the store that cannot behave like a cached blog: cart, checkout, account, orders, stock, payment callbacks, scheduled actions and database writes. Monthly visits or product count alone do not tell you how much server the store needs.

For the broader WordPress workload, see VPS for WordPress. For the central server-buying path, see VPS for website.

item.title: VPS for WordPress
item.description:
VPS for WordPress is useful when WordPress needs more control, isolation or server-level features than shared hosting can provide. The VPS should be sized around uncached PHP work, database demand, plugins, background jobs, storage growth and the services that run beside WordPress, not around a monthly visitor number.

For the broader server decision, see VPS for website.

item.title: VPS Monitoring
item.description:
VPS Monitoring should answer more than “is the server up?” A production monitoring baseline needs external availability checks, historical host metrics, service/application health, logs, actionable alerts and a named response owner.

A VPS can respond to ping while Nginx is broken, the database is stalled, the disk is full or the TLS certificate is about to expire. Monitoring therefore has to cover both the server and the user-facing website.

For the broader server decision, see VPS for website.

item.title: VPS Security Checklist
item.description:
VPS Security Checklist is a prioritized hardening pass for an internet-facing self-managed server. The goal is not to make a VPS “100% secure.” The goal is to remove avoidable attack surface, protect privileged access, keep software maintained, make recovery possible and verify that somebody actually owns the security work.

The safest order matters: preserve a recovery path first, verify a second administrative login, inventory exposed services, then tighten SSH and firewall rules.

item.title: VPS sizing for website
item.description:
VPS sizing for a website should start with the workload that reaches the origin server, not with a monthly visitor count. Cacheability, simultaneous dynamic requests, PHP or application workers, database activity, background jobs, control-panel overhead and storage growth determine how much CPU, RAM and disk the website actually needs.

For the broader purchase decision, see VPS for website.

item.title: VPS vs Shared Hosting
item.description:
VPS vs Shared Hosting is not a simple “small site vs big site” decision. Shared hosting is usually easier because the provider operates the server stack. A VPS gives you more control and a more isolated virtual environment, but you or an administrator must operate the guest server.

The correct decision is usually one of four outcomes: stay on shared hosting, optimize first, move to VPS, or move only with managed/administration help.

item.title: VPS with Control Panel
item.description:
VPS with Control Panel means running a web-hosting or server-management interface on top of a VPS so routine tasks can be handled from a browser instead of only through SSH or RDP. The important decision is not “which dashboard looks nicest?” It is whether you need a panel at all, and which panel model matches the websites, users, mail, operating system and support model you actually need.

For the broader server-buying decision, see VPS for website.

item.title: Website migration to VPS
item.description:
Website migration to VPS is safest when the new server is built and tested while the old host is still serving traffic. Inventory the current stack, size the destination, copy and validate the site, control the final data changes, switch DNS last, then monitor both environments until the old host can be retired.

This page assumes the domain and public URL structure stay the same. If the domain or paths also change, URL mapping and permanent redirects become a separate migration job.
